newsitem.title: USA: Lawyer denies Michael Jackson spied on staff.
newsitem.headline: Lawyer denies Michael Jackson spied on staff.

text.p: A lawyer for singer Michael Jackson denied in court on Tuesday that the self-proclaimed "King of Pop" spied on employees at his Neverland Ranch.
"There have been terrible allegations here about eavesdropping. There was none, no bugging of the house, no bugging of the telephones," attorney Steve Cochran told the jury in Jackson's civil trial.

Three former bodyguards, a maid and an administrative assistant sued Jackson and six of his aides, alleging the entertainer and aides imposed intolerable working conditions on them and forced them from their jobs in retaliation for cooperating with investigators in a child-molestation probe of Jackson.
The group charged that Jackson used recording devices at the ranch in an attempt to find out what they knew about the abuse allegations.

In 1993 a 13-year-old boy sued Jackson, charging the singer molested him. The lawsuit was settled out of court for a reported $15 million and Jackson, who denied any wrongdoing, was never charged with a crime.
In his opening statement, Cochran said, "the vast majority of employees were loyal, dedicated, enjoyed working at the ranch and have no problems with their jobs"
He said Jackson did have certain equipment at the ranch outside Santa Barbara, but only to protect his own security.
There was a clock with a camera in the face to see who was outside his bedroom, a scanner to monitor shortwave calls, and mirrors for looking underneath cars, Cochran said.
The lawyer said "there was a certain amount of sexual banter" at the ranch, which employs around 100 people and includes Jackson's own private zoo.
Speaking of the plaintiffs individually, Cochran referred to maid Adrian McManus, as "the house jester," who was the "leader of the sexual banter."
The attorney also told the jury McManus "bragged to other staff about how much work she didn't have to do."

She had a key to Jackson's bedroom and told co-workers she spent much of her time lying on his bed watching television, Cochran said, adding that she became angry when Jackson changed the locks on his bedroom door and gave the key to someone else.

The attorney said all employees must sign a confidentiality provision when they start working at Neverland that binds them from publicly discussing Jackson's business affairs, operations or personal life.
"This provision is designed to keep the home a home in terms of privacy," Cochran said.
Jackson was not in court on Tuesday and it was not clear whether he would testify in person.

Last week a lawyer for the former employees said Jackson's lieutenants knew they could not fire the plaintiffs because they could be sued. So they decided to make their lives so miserable they would quit on their own.
